full_text_en:
Guiding Case No. 232: MouMu Industrial Co., Ltd. v. PaMou Shipping Co., Ltd. — dispute over contract of carriage of goods by sea

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on November 25, 2024)

Keywords civil / contract of carriage of goods by sea / burden of proof for cargo damage / endorsement on bill of lading

Ruling Gist

Pursuant to Article 76 of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China, if the carrier fails to make an endorsement on the bill of lading regarding the apparent bad order of the goods at the time of loading, the carrier shall bear the adverse consequences arising therefrom. However, whether the carrier has truthfully endorsed the apparent condition of the goods shall be comprehensively evaluated based on whether the carrier had the objective conditions to observe the apparent condition of the goods at the time of issuing the bill of lading, and whether the judgment made by the carrier conformed to the usual standard.

Basic Facts

The plaintiff, MouMu Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as MouMu Industrial), alleged that: MouMu Industrial imported a batch of corn distiller's dried grains with solubles (hereinafter referred to as DDGS) from the United States, which were carried by the vessel "MouBa" owned by PaMou Shipping Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as PaMou Shipping). PaMou Shipping issued a bill of lading for the goods in question, recording a weight of 54,999.642 metric tons. The goods arrived at Xinsha Port, Guangzhou. During discharge, it was discovered that the goods in some compartments had severe discoloration, caking, and a burnt smell. After commissioning relevant inspection agencies to conduct surveys and tests, the Hunter L value and crude protein content of the goods were found to be seriously inconsistent with the original quality of the goods, with a total damaged quantity of 20,931.98 metric tons. Therefore, MouMu Industrial requested the court to order PaMou Shipping to compensate for the losses and interest, and to bear the litigation costs.

The defendant, PaMou Shipping, argued that: The goods in question were not discolored or damaged. The Hunter L value requires professional laboratory testing, and the master and carrier had no obligation to test this quality indicator of the goods, nor to make an endorsement on the bill of lading. The goods in question already had different colors at the time of loading, and the crew had exercised reasonable diligence in caring for the goods, without causing discoloration or deepening of color during transportation. The losses claimed by MouMu Industrial were unfounded, and PaMou Shipping requested the court to dismiss MouMu Industrial's claims.

The court ascertained through trial that: MouMu Industrial entered into a sales contract with MouLiang (USA) Co., Ltd. to purchase DDGS, with a total weight of 50,000 metric tons and a Hunter L value of 50 or above. On August 26, 2015, NanMou Agency Co., Ltd. issued a bill of lading on behalf of the master of the vessel "MouBa". The bill of lading was headed as North American Grain Bill of Lading, to be used concurrently with the North American Grain 1973 Form Voyage Charter Party. The goods were loaded by LanMou Trading Group on behalf of MouLiang (USA) Co., Ltd., and the goods appeared to be in apparent good order at the time of loading. The consignee was to order, with the notify party being MouMu Industrial. The description and stowage of the goods were: DDGS, 54,999.642 metric tons, stowed in compartments 1 to 7, clean bill of lading, freight as per charter party dated March 11, 2015, transportation terms on reverse side, weight, quality, and quantity stated by shipper unknown. PaMou Shipping was the bareboat charterer of the vessel "MouBa". LaMou Maritime Group issued a quality report for the DDGS on August 28, 2015, stating that samples taken at the loading port showed the Hunter L value of the goods loaded on the "MouBa" to be 50.8.

On October 14, 2015, the "MouBa" arrived at Xinsha Port, Guangzhou, and began discharging. During the discharge process, MouMu Industrial claimed that cargo damage had occurred and filed a claim against the carrier. For this purpose, MouMu Industrial commissioned China MouMou Certification Group Guangdong Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as China MouMou Certification) to inspect the 20,931.98 metric tons of DDGS stored in warehouses 6-2B and 7-4B. China MouMou Certification issued an inspection report on March 14, 2016, which recorded that inspectors went to the warehouses at Xinsha Port, Guangzhou, on October 24, 2015, to visually inspect the 20,931.98 metric tons of DDGS declared by MouMu Industrial, stored in warehouses 6-2B and 7-4B, and collected representative samples. The inspection showed a Hunter L value of 42.5.

Dalian MouJie Marine Insurance Surveyors Co., Ltd., commissioned on behalf of the shipowner, boarded the "MouBa" from October 16 to 24, 2015, to conduct inspection and investigation, and arranged for inspectors from TongMou Standard Technical Services Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as TongMou Standard Technical Services) to supervise the discharge, inspect the condition of the goods, and take samples. During the inspection, the inspectors found no abnormalities affecting the vessel's seaworthiness and cargo-worthiness, and the watertight integrity of the vessel's cargo holds was good. TongMou Standard Technical Services issued an inspection report stating that inspectors supervised the discharge of the goods in question at Xinsha Port, Guangzhou, from October 19 to 24, 2015, and systematically collected small samples in the warehouse. The mixed sample inspection of the whole cargo showed a Hunter L value of 48.66.

Furthermore, according to the loading port inspection report, loading records, and loading photos from August 2015, part of the goods in question was loaded at the dock by conveyor belt, and another part was loaded by grab from barges. At the time of loading, the goods from the 42 barges had different colors, and these goods were loaded into various cargo holds of the "MouBa".

Judgment

The Guangzhou Maritime Court rendered the civil judgment (2016) Yue 72 Min Chu No. 705 on December 29, 2018: 1. PaMou Shipping shall compensate MouMu Industrial Co., Ltd. for cargo losses of RMB 9,862,112.57 and interest; 2. All other claims of MouMu Industrial Co., Ltd. were dismissed. After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, PaMou Shipping appealed. The Guangdong High People's Court rendered the civil judgment (2019) Yue Min Zhong No. 807 on April 8, 2020: dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment. After the second-instance judgment was pronounced, PaMou Shipping applied for retrial. The Supreme People's Court accepted the retrial and rendered the civil judgment (2022) Zui Gao Fa Min Zai No. 14 on June 21, 2023: 1. Setting aside the civil judgment (2019) Yue Min Zhong No. 807 of the Guangdong High People's Court and the civil judgment (2016) Yue 72 Min Chu No. 705 of the Guangzhou Maritime Court; 2. Dismissing all claims of MouMu Industrial Co., Ltd.

Reasoning

This case involves a dispute over cargo damage under a contract of carriage of goods by sea, with two key issues: (1) whether the goods in question suffered damage during the carrier's period of responsibility; and (2) whether PaMou Shipping should be liable for compensation due to its failure to truthfully endorse the bill of lading.

1. Whether the goods in question suffered damage during the carrier's period of responsibility.

MouMu Industrial failed to effectively prove that the color and quality of the goods in question changed during the period of responsibility of the carrier, PaMou Shipping, resulting in losses. Specifically:

1.1. There is no internationally unified grading system or quality standard for DDGS. The Hunter L value is a test value reflecting the brightness of the goods' color. Color depth may be related to raw materials, production process, temperature, etc., and may also deepen due to heat source heating or excessive moisture content during transportation. Therefore, different colors do not necessarily indicate quality issues.

1.2. The scope of goods, sampling and sample preparation methods, and testing standards used by China MouMou Certification and LaMou Maritime Group were different, and their conclusions were not absolutely comparable. The inspection report of China MouMou Certification was insufficient to prove that the color of the goods in question changed during transportation, causing damage.

1.3. The evidence submitted by PaMou Shipping showed that the goods in question already had different colors at the time of loading and were stowed in different cargo holds of the vessel, and the condition of the goods at the discharge port was substantially consistent with that at the loading port.

1.4. There was no evidence of any defect in the vessel's cargo-worthiness, nor any evidence that the carrier improperly cared for the goods, resulting in color deepening due to heat source heating or excessive moisture content.

2. Whether PaMou Shipping should be liable for compensation due to its failure to truthfully endorse the bill of lading.

MouMu Industrial claimed that PaMou Shipping failed to carefully verify the apparent condition of the goods at the loading port and failed to truthfully endorse on the bill of lading that the goods in question already had a bad condition of mixed light and dark colors at the time of loading, and should therefore bear the losses caused to MouMu Industrial by the failure to truthfully endorse. Article 76 of the Maritime Code provides: "If the carrier or the person issuing the bill of lading on his behalf fails to make an endorsement on the bill of lading regarding the apparent order of the goods, the goods shall be deemed to be in apparent good order." Accordingly, the carrier has the right to make endorsements regarding what it considers to be the apparent bad order of the goods at the time of loading. If no endorsement is made, the carrier shall bear the adverse consequences arising therefrom. Therefore, the carrier shall exercise its right of endorsement on the bill of lading appropriately and carefully. In this case, whether PaMou Shipping should be liable for compensation due to its failure to truthfully endorse the bill of lading shall be comprehensively evaluated based on whether it had the objective conditions to observe the apparent condition of the goods, and whether the judgment made conformed to the usual standard.

First, the goods in question were bulk cargo. According to the loading port records, they were loaded by conveyor belt and grab, respectively. During loading, the cargo holds were full of dust, and the dock covered the hatches with canvas to prevent dust pollution. Under these circumstances, it was difficult for the crew to clearly and fully observe the apparent condition of all the goods, and there were no objective conditions to suspect any abnormality in the apparent condition of the goods.

Second, the master and crew are not experts in identifying DDGS, and they do not have professional judgment ability regarding color brightness. Moreover, the Hunter L value requires precise testing with laboratory instruments, and it is difficult to distinguish differences by naked eye when the values are close. It is reasonable for the carrier to judge the goods as being in apparent good order based on normal knowledge and usual judgment standards. It was not improper for PaMou Shipping to issue a bill of lading recording "goods appeared to be in apparent good order at the time of loading" based on the loading situation.

Third, DDGS may have multiple colors due to various factors such as raw materials and processing methods. Different colors indicate different intrinsic qualities, but they are not manifestations of damage to the goods and do not represent apparent bad order. The law does not impose an obligation on the carrier to endorse the intrinsic quality of the goods being transported. Therefore, the color of DDGS is not within the carrier's statutory scope of endorsement. Furthermore, the shipper did not specifically declare the color requirements of the goods in question to PaMou Shipping at the time of booking. Even if the goods in question had different colors at the loading port, it was not improper for PaMou Shipping and its agent to receive the goods and issue a clean bill of lading recording "goods appeared to be in apparent good order at the time of loading."

In conclusion, MouMu Industrial's claim that PaMou Shipping should bear liability for failure to truthfully endorse lacks factual and legal basis, and PaMou Shipping should not be liable for compensation.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Articles 46 and 76 of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China.
